title: Thinking Verbs
objectives: I can name eight things my mind does when I read and learn.
I can tell what I noticed, wondered, and predicted about a text.
I can use thinking verbs to say what I did in my mind.
I can tell the difference between guess, predict, and believe.
rationale: Reading and science depend on verbs that name thinking. Second graders can say what they did with their hands, but they need words for what they did in their minds. The eight verbs follow a thinking path: noticing and asking (notice, wonder), looking ahead (predict, guess, decide), and knowing and believing (believe, understand, realize). Children use them to say what they thought before, during, and after a read-aloud or a science activity, which is the first step to talking about their own learning.

words.def: To see or hear something and pay attention.
words.ex: I noticed a bird's nest in the tree.
words.ex2: Did you notice the new poster on the wall?
words.nonExample: Walking past a sign without looking is not noticing it.

apps.academic: Scientists notice details before they ask questions.
apps.spoken: I notice that the plant is taller today.
apps.writing: Use notice to tell what a character saw or heard.

cloze.s: Maya began to ___ small tracks in the mud near the pond.

cloze2.s: Did you ___ that the leaves are turning red and orange?

misuse.s: I noticed the loud bell, but I did not see it or hear it at all.
misuse.why: To notice means to see or hear something, so not hearing it means no noticing.

visual.alt: A pair of eyes looking at a bird in a tree.

words.def: To make up your mind about something.
words.ex: We could not decide between the red paint and the blue paint.
words.ex2: Mia decided to read a book about space.
words.nonExample: Letting someone else choose is not deciding for yourself.

apps.academic: Good readers decide what to do when they do not know a word.
apps.spoken: I cannot decide what to eat.
apps.writing: Use decide to tell what a character chose to do.

cloze.s: It is hard to ___ which flavor of ice cream to order when there are so many.

cloze2.s: After thinking about it, Tom ___ to walk to school instead of riding the bus.

misuse.s: Ben decided on a blue shirt and never chose anything at all.
misuse.why: To decide is to choose, so he cannot have chosen nothing.

visual.alt: A child with a hand on her chin beside a pair of scales.

words.def: To think about something and want to know.
words.ex: I wonder why the sky is blue.
words.ex2: Kai wondered what lived at the bottom of the lake.
words.nonExample: Knowing every answer already is not wondering.

apps.academic: Scientists write what they notice and what they wonder.
apps.spoken: I wonder how birds find their way.
apps.writing: Use wonder to start a question about something you want to learn.

cloze.s: Lena looked at the stars and began to ___ how far away they were.

cloze2.s: I ___ what the dog is dreaming about while it sleeps.

misuse.s: I wonder what time it is, and I already know it is exactly noon.
misuse.why: To wonder is to want to know, so you do not wonder about something you already know.

visual.alt: A thought bubble above a girl looking at the stars.

words.def: To say what you think will happen next.
words.ex: Can you predict what the story will say next?
words.ex2: Omar predicted that the ice would melt in the sun.
words.nonExample: Telling what already happened is not predicting.

apps.academic: Predict what will happen before you turn the page.
apps.spoken: I predict that it will snow tonight.
apps.writing: Use predict with a clue: I predict this because the text says so.

cloze.s: Look at the dark clouds and ___ what the weather will be like soon.

cloze2.s: Before we dropped the stone in the water, Eva ___ that it would sink.

misuse.s: I predicted the winner of the game yesterday after it was already over.
misuse.why: To predict is to say what will happen next, not after it already happened.

visual.alt: A glass ball next to a gray cloud.

words.ex: I believe that you did your best.
words.ex2: Do you believe the weather report?
words.nonExample: Knowing something is false is not believing it.

apps.academic: Give a reason for what you believe.
apps.writing: Use believe with a reason: I believe this because the text says so.

cloze.s: I ___ my friend because she always tells the truth.

cloze2.s: He did not ___ the story about a dragon in the garden.

misuse.s: I believe the grass is purple, and I know it is green.
misuse.why: To believe is to think something is true, so you cannot believe it when you know it is false.

visual.alt: A thought bubble beside a thumbs up.

words.ex: Now I understand how to add big numbers.
words.ex2: Did you understand the directions on the board?
words.nonExample: Not knowing what a word means is not understanding it.

apps.academic: Ask a question when you do not understand.
apps.spoken: I understand the rules of the game.
apps.writing: Use understand to tell what a character knows after thinking.

cloze.s: I read the page twice so I would ___ the hard words.

cloze2.s: When Ms. Park explained the game slowly, everyone began to ___ it.

misuse.s: I understand the story, but I have no idea what it says.
misuse.why: To understand is to know what something means, so you cannot have no idea.

visual.alt: A light bulb beside a brain.

words.def: To say an answer without being sure.
words.ex: Can you guess how many beans are in the jar?
words.ex2: I guessed the answer, and I got it right.
words.nonExample: Knowing the exact answer is not guessing.

apps.academic: It is okay to guess, and then check your answer.
apps.writing: Use guess when you give an answer you have not checked yet.

cloze.s: I did not know the answer, so I had to ___.

cloze2.s: Can you ___ my age if I give you three clues?

misuse.s: I guessed the answer because I knew it perfectly and was totally sure.
misuse.why: To guess is to answer without being sure.

visual.alt: A die beside a question mark.

words.def: To suddenly understand or notice something.
words.ex: Ana realized she had left her lunch at home.
words.ex2: I realized the answer when I saw the picture.
words.nonExample: Knowing something all along is not realizing it.

apps.academic: A character may realize something at the end of a story.
apps.spoken: I just realized that I forgot my book.
apps.writing: Use realize for the moment a character understands something new.

cloze.s: At the door, Dev began to ___ that he had forgotten his keys.

cloze2.s: When the bell rang, I ___ I had been reading for an hour.

misuse.s: I realized something that I had known for years and was never surprised.
misuse.why: To realize is to understand something suddenly, not to know it for years.

visual.alt: A light bulb above a surprised face.

passage.title: The Mystery Seed
paras: Leo planted a seed and began to wonder what would grow. He guessed it was a sunflower, but Maya said, "I predict it will be a bean." Leo decided to watch it every day.
On Friday, he noticed a small green shoot. Soon he realized the plant had two round leaves, like a bean. Now he could understand why Maya was right, and he began to believe her.

qs.q: What does "predict" mean in the story?
choices: say what you think will happen
qs.why: Maya said what she thought would happen: the plant would be a bean.

qs.q: What did Leo notice on Friday?
qs.why: The story says he noticed a small green shoot.

qs.q: Who was right about the plant?
qs.why: Leo understood why Maya was right when he saw the bean leaves.

write.prompt: Write what you noticed and what you wonder about something outside.

study.task: Act out each verb without talking and let your partner name it. Then sort the verbs into three groups: noticing and asking, looking ahead, and knowing and believing.

sentences: Write a sentence about something you noticed on the way to school.
Write a sentence that tells what you predict will happen tomorrow.
Write a sentence about a time you realized you made a mistake.

given: He wanted to know what would grow.
combine.model: Leo planted a seed and began to wonder what would grow.

given: She saw her lunch was missing.
combine.model: Ana realized her lunch was missing when she looked in her bag.

discuss: What is the difference between a guess and a prediction?
What do you do when you do not understand something in a book?
produce.explain: Explain how believe and understand are different. Give an example of each.

argue.prompt: Is it okay to guess on a hard question? Say yes or no and give a reason.
argue.frame: I think it is ___ to guess because ___.

constructed.prompt: Look at a plant or an animal. Tell what you notice and what you wonder.
constructed.model: I notice that the leaf has small holes. I wonder what ate it.

constructed.prompt: Tell what you predict will happen next in a story you know. Then tell what a character might realize.
look: gives a reason for the prediction
constructed.model: I predict the turtle will win the race because he keeps going. The hare might realize he should not nap.

teacher.overview: Children learn eight verbs that name thinking and use them before, during, and after reading or science work. Start with notice and wonder, then add predict, guess, and decide. Revisit curious, journey, and shallow by asking what a curious character might notice on a journey.

notes.va.notice.v: Noticing is the first step in science and reading. Use a routine with a picture: What do you notice? Children often say see; push toward notice a detail.
notes.va.decide.v: Decide is to choose. Use a real choice with two options and model the thinking. Spanish speakers have the cognate decidir.
notes.va.wonder.v: Teach the verb sense I wonder. The noun sense (a wonder) is a different use and can wait. Link to the question the child wants answered.
notes.va.predict.v: Predict needs a reason. Use clues from a picture or the cover. Spanish speakers have predecir. Contrast with guess: a prediction uses clues.
notes.va.believe.v: Believe needs a reason, too. Be careful with beliefs about families or faith; use story examples.
notes.va.understand.v: Understand is about meaning. Teach a signal: thumbs up, sideways, or down. Children often say yes without understanding, so ask them to tell it in their own words.
notes.va.guess.v: Guess is an answer you are not sure of. Guessing is fine in a safe class; then check. Contrast with predict: a guess may have no clues.
notes.va.realize.v: Realize is a sudden understanding. Use a story moment: the character looks in a bag and realizes the lunch is gone. Practice with a pause in a read-aloud.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The cover shows dark clouds. I predict it will rain in this story because the clouds are dark. I notice the dog is under a tree. I wonder if it is hiding from the rain.'
discuss: What do you notice first when you open a new book?
When did you realize something while reading this week?
misconceptions: Children may use guess and predict as the same. A prediction uses clues.
Some children think understand means yes. Ask them to explain.
Children may say wonder only as a noun, as in a wonder of the world.
extend: Add a notice, wonder, and predict chart to a science corner.
Retell a story using three thinking verbs for a character.
teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit curious, journey, and shallow: a curious child may notice something on a journey, wonder about a shallow stream, and predict what is in it.

wida.oral: Look at a picture with a partner. Take turns saying one thing you notice, one thing you wonder, and one prediction.

needsReview: Spanish glosses (notar, decidir, preguntarse, predecir, creer, entender, adivinar, darse cuenta) not reviewed by a native speaker; creer and entender are the usual forms for believe and understand.
wonder, guess, and notice have other senses (a wonder, a guess, a notice); only the verb sense is taught.
